title: Forward Deployed Engineering 101 — Kevin Bai, Anthropic, ex Palantir & Rippling Founding FDE

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 48%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk is about a delivery model built around developer platforms with shared primitives. Palantir Foundry, AWS primitives, and the concept of a reusable platform substrate are central to the discussion, placing it firmly in the developer-platforms domain.

summary:
Kevin Bai (Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic, ex-Palantir and founding FDE at Rippling) delivers a 101 on Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) at the AI Engineer World's Fair. FDE is a go-to-market model for selling a technically complex platform to a non-technical buyer: instead of selling just a product or services, you sell an outcome by loaning trained engineers who assemble real solutions on top of a reusable platform. Kevin grounds this in Palantir's Foundry, which centralizes enterprise data into an ontology ("data proper nouns") that serves as the platform substrate. Selling the platform alone failed because customers wanted business outcomes, not organized data, and faced a high training tax.

Kevin presents a 2x2 framework: FDE is only necessary when selling something very technical to a non-technical buyer. If your buyer is technical (GitHub, Datadog) or your product is merely configurable (Rippling, Slack), you don't need FDE. The business case is compelling: Palantir leads public SaaS in ACV at ~$4M, dwarfing ServiceNow at ~$1.2M and Workday at ~$600K, with no other public SaaS cracking $500K.

The critical distinction from a dev shop is that FDEs never build from scratch—they assemble on shared primitives. Building bespoke code per customer creates unmaintainable sprawl. Kevin offers two gating questions: do you have a corner case requiring a technically complicated GTM to a non-technical buyer, and do you have or will you invest in a platform with shared primitives?

Kevin then addresses what changed in the AI era: AI has made building dramatically easier, and nearly every platform is now agentic and customizable. This means customers increasingly won't understand what you do, making FDE more relevant—not because the industry discovered Palantir's model, but because the nature of software business itself changed. In Q&A, Kevin covers primitive granularity (depends on use case; AWS's DynamoDB as example), the bespoke-stays/generalizable-goes-to-platform principle, and FDE as a scout for new product opportunities. He closes with the ideal FDE profile: a customer-facing software engineer—someone you'd hire as an engineer and also trust in front of a customer.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts form a coherent narrative about how complex platforms reach non-technical buyers. FDE, shared primitives, and the bespoke-to-platform migration pattern define the engineering delivery model. The ontology and primitive granularity concepts describe the platform substrate that makes assembly possible. The two-axis framework and ACV metric provide the decision logic and economic evidence for when this model works. The agentic platform and AI-era acceleration concepts explain why this model is becoming more relevant, not less, as AI makes platforms more powerful but also harder for non-technical buyers to understand. Together, they describe a complete loop: AI creates the market conditions (agentic, customizable, incomprehensible-to-buyers platforms), FDE provides the delivery mechanism (loan engineers who assemble on shared primitives), the platform provides the scalability (shared primitives prevent dev-shop sprawl), and ACV provides the economic validation (Palantir's outlier contracts prove the model works commercially). The bespoke-to-platform migration ensures the system improves over time, with FDE serving as both delivery mechanism and product scout.
temporalContext: The video was published on July 28, 2026, at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Kevin Bai joined Anthropic in mid-June 2026 (per his LinkedIn announcement), having previously been at Rippling from August 2025 to early 2026 and at Palantir from 2021 to 2025. The talk reflects the state of the AI industry in mid-2026, when agentic platforms were becoming mainstream and companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks were beginning to adopt FDE patterns modeled on Palantir's playbook. The ACV data cited reflects public SaaS financials as of mid-2026. Palantir's Foundry launched in 2016, and the FDE model originated in the early 2010s, providing roughly a decade of track record by the time of this talk.
takeaways: FDE is specifically for selling a technically complex product to a non-technical buyer—other combinations call for different go-to-market motions.
The customer buys an outcome, not a product or a service; you loan engineers who build a real solution on your platform.
Palantir leads public SaaS in ACV at ~$4M, far above ServiceNow ($1.2M) and Workday ($600K); no other public SaaS cracks $500K ACV.
The defining ingredient of a real FDE program is a platform of shared primitives—engineers assemble, never build from scratch.
Two gating questions before starting FDE: must you sell something complicated to a non-technical buyer, and do you have or will you invest in a platform?
AI has made building dramatically easier; nearly every platform is now agentic and customizable, pulling FDE toward the center of how software is sold.
Bespoke work stays on the FDE side; generalizable work should move to the platform over time. FDE also scouts ahead for new product opportunities.
The ideal FDE is a customer-facing software engineer—someone you'd hire as an engineer and also trust in front of a customer.

concepts.name: Agentic platforms
concepts.explanation: AI-powered platforms that are agentic and customizable, meaning they can take autonomous actions and be tailored to specific use cases. Kevin argues that nearly every platform is now becoming agentic.
concepts.importance: The rise of agentic platforms is what makes FDE more relevant in the AI era—customers increasingly cannot self-serve or understand what the platform does, creating the exact market conditions FDE was designed for.

concepts.name: AI-era acceleration of FDE relevance
concepts.explanation: AI has made building dramatically easier and platforms more customizable, which paradoxically increases the need for FDE because the gap between what platforms can do and what non-technical buyers can understand widens.
concepts.importance: Explains why FDE is not a legacy model but is becoming more central to how AI-era software is sold and deployed.

concepts.name: AI companies adopting FDE patterns
concepts.explanation: Companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks are adopting FDE patterns modeled on Palantir's playbook, including ontology-based deployment and outcome-based selling for AI platforms.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that FDE is not just a Palantir phenomenon but is becoming a standard go-to-market model for AI platform companies facing the non-technical buyer problem.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
concepts.explanation: A go-to-market and engineering delivery model where a company loans trained engineers to customers who build real solutions on top of a reusable platform, selling an outcome rather than a product or service. Pioneered by Palantir with Foundry.
concepts.importance: Central concept of the talk; defines when and how a technical platform company should deploy engineers to close the gap between complex technology and non-technical buyers.

concepts.name: Platform with shared primitives
concepts.explanation: A platform of reusable building blocks (primitives) that FDEs assemble against rather than building from scratch. This is the defining ingredient that separates a real FDE program from a custom dev shop.
concepts.importance: Without shared primitives, FDE devolves into unmaintainable bespoke code per customer. The platform is what makes FDE scalable and economically viable.

concepts.name: Bespoke-to-platform migration
concepts.explanation: The principle that customer-specific (bespoke) work stays on the FDE side while generalizable patterns should be extracted and moved to the platform over time. This creates a feedback loop where FDE work feeds platform evolution.
concepts.importance: Ensures the platform grows from real customer needs while preventing code sprawl. Also positions FDE as a scout for new product opportunities.

concepts.name: Two-axis GTM decision framework
concepts.explanation: A 2x2 matrix mapping product complexity (technical vs. configurable) against buyer technical sophistication (technical vs. non-technical). FDE is only necessary in the quadrant where a very technical product is sold to a non-technical buyer.
concepts.importance: Provides a clear decision rule for when FDE is the right go-to-market motion versus alternatives like DevRel or sales-led growth.

concepts.name: Average Contract Value (ACV) as a software business metric
concepts.explanation: ACV measures the average revenue per customer contract. Palantir leads public SaaS at ~$4M ACV, far exceeding ServiceNow ($1.2M) and Workday ($600K), with no other public SaaS cracking $500K.
concepts.importance: Provides quantitative evidence that the FDE model produces outlier economics compared to other enterprise SaaS go-to-market motions.

concepts.name: Ontology as platform substrate
concepts.explanation: Palantir Foundry's ontology centralizes enterprise data into 'data proper nouns'—structured representations of business entities and relationships—that serve as the building blocks FDEs assemble against.
concepts.importance: The ontology is the technical foundation that makes FDE possible at Palantir; it provides the shared primitives that differentiate FDE from a dev shop.

concepts.name: Primitive granularity
concepts.explanation: The level of abstraction at which platform primitives are exposed. Kevin uses AWS's DynamoDB as an example of robust primitives serving a broad customer base. Granularity depends on use case and customer diversity.
concepts.importance: Determines how broadly applicable the platform is and how much assembly work FDEs must do per customer. Too fine-grained increases effort; too coarse reduces flexibility.

concepts.name: Customer-facing software engineer (FDE profile)
concepts.explanation: The ideal FDE is someone you would hire as a software engineer on your team but also trust in front of a customer. This dual bar—engineering competence plus customer trust—defines the hiring profile.
concepts.importance: Defines who can succeed in FDE; the role requires both technical depth and interpersonal/communication skills that typical engineering roles do not demand.

concepts.name: Design partnership at enterprise scale
concepts.explanation: FDE is essentially a design partnership—collaborative solution-building between vendor and customer—scaled to enterprise, where the vendor loans engineers rather than just consulting.
concepts.importance: Frames FDE as a natural extension of product design collaboration rather than a purely transactional services engagement.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Kevin Bai introduces himself as member of technical staff at Anthropic on applied AI, previously first hire on Rippling's FDE team (grown to ~25 in a year), and earlier at Palantir. He frames the talk around the history and function of FDE.

sections.title: What Palantir does and where FDE fits
sections.summary: Palantir's Foundry centralizes data into an ontology and enables app building. Selling technology alone fell short because customers wanted business outcomes, not organized data, and faced a training tax. The solution: sell an outcome by loaning trained engineers who build on the platform.

sections.title: The 2x2: when FDE is necessary
sections.summary: Kevin maps product complexity against buyer technical sophistication. FDE is only needed when selling something very technical to a non-technical buyer, as Palantir did with Fortune 500 companies lacking engineering depth. Fine dining waiter analogy: engineers cater to needs and solve the problem.

sections.title: Business case: landing large contracts
sections.summary: Palantir leads public SaaS in ACV at ~$4M, followed by ServiceNow at $1.2M and Workday at $600K. No other public SaaS company cracks $500K ACV, demonstrating the commercial effectiveness of the FDE model.

sections.title: FDE as design partnership scaled to enterprise
sections.summary: FDE is a design partnership scaled to enterprise. The trap is building bespoke code per customer, which creates unmaintainable sprawl. A real FDE program builds on a platform of shared primitives; otherwise it is just a dev shop.

sections.title: How to start: two questions
sections.summary: Two gating questions: do you genuinely need FDE (must sell something complicated to a non-technical buyer), and do you have or will you invest in a platform with shared primitives? Without both, consider DevRel or SLG instead.

sections.title: What has changed since Palantir
sections.summary: Kevin explains that AI has made building dramatically easier, and nearly every platform is now agentic and customizable. This means customers increasingly won't understand what you do, making FDE more relevant—not because the industry discovered Palantir's model, but because the nature of software business itself changed.

sections.title: Q&A: primitives, collaboration, platform split, and FDE profile
sections.summary: Kevin fields questions on primitive granularity (depends on use case; AWS's DynamoDB as example of robust primitives for a broad customer base), collaboration patterns (multiple FDEs on a project avoids single points of failure), what goes on the platform vs FDE side (bespoke stays with customer, generalizable moves to platform; FDE scouts ahead for new product opportunities), and the ideal FDE profile: a customer-facing software engineer you'd hire as an engineer and trust in front of a customer.

organization.name: Palantir Technologies
organization.summary: Palantir Technologies is a publicly traded software company (NYSE: PLTR) that builds and deploys enterprise software platforms serving as central operating systems for commercial and government customers. Its flagship product, Palantir Foundry, is an ontology-powered data operations platform that centralizes enterprise data, logic, action, and security into a unified representation. Palantir pioneered the Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) model, in which customer-facing software engineers build solutions on top of Foundry's shared primitives rather than from scratch. The talk's speaker, Kevin Bai, was a Forward Deployed Software Engineer at Palantir (2021-2025) and uses Palantir as the primary case study for FDE. Palantir leads public SaaS companies in average contract value at approximately $4 million.
organization.status: Active, publicly traded on NYSE as PLTR. Foundry continues as a core commercial product with SaaS and on-premises plans, integrated with AIP (AI Platform) and Apollo (continuous delivery). The company continues to develop Foundry through the FDE methodology.

technologies.label: Palantir Foundry
technologies.summary: Palantir Foundry is the ontology-powered data operations platform that serves as the central technology substrate in the talk. Kevin Bai describes Foundry as centralizing enterprise data into an ontology (which he calls 'data proper nouns') that enables forward deployed engineers to assemble customer-specific applications without building from scratch. Foundry is part of an integrated Enterprise Operating System alongside AIP (AI) and Apollo (continuous delivery). Verified through multiple first-party Palantir sources as a live commercial product, Foundry's commercial success—Palantir leads public SaaS in ACV at approximately $4 million—is the quantitative evidence Kevin uses to argue the FDE model works.
technologies.role: Central platform technology discussed as the origin and exemplar of the FDE model. Foundry's Ontology system is described as the substrate that makes assembly-based engineering possible, and its commercial performance is used as quantitative proof that FDE produces outlier economics.

technologies.label: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
technologies.summary: Forward Deployed Engineering is the go-to-market and engineering delivery methodology that is the central subject of the talk. Pioneered by Palantir in the early 2010s, FDE involves loaning trained engineers to customers who build real solutions on top of a reusable platform, selling an outcome rather than a product or service. Kevin frames FDE as a design partnership scaled to enterprise, distinct from a dev shop because FDEs assemble on shared primitives rather than building from scratch. The model requires two conditions: a technically complex product sold to a non-technical buyer, and a platform with shared primitives. Externally verified that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks are now adopting FDE patterns modeled on Palantir's playbook.
technologies.role: Primary subject of the talk. Kevin explains when FDE is needed (2x2 framework and gating questions), how it works (assemble on shared primitives), what differentiates it from a dev shop, how it has changed in the AI era (agentic platforms), and the ideal FDE profile (customer-facing software engineer).

technologies.label: Platform with shared primitives
technologies.summary: A platform architecture based on reusable building blocks (primitives) that forward deployed engineers assemble against rather than building from scratch. Kevin Bai argues this is the defining ingredient that separates a real FDE program from a custom dev shop: without shared primitives, each FDE builds bespoke code, creating unmaintainable sprawl. The granularity of primitives depends on use case and customer diversity; Kevin cites AWS DynamoDB as an example of robust primitives serving a broad customer base. The bespoke-to-platform migration principle ensures that generalizable work moves from the FDE side to the platform over time.
technologies.role: Central architectural concept that defines what makes FDE work. Kevin uses it to differentiate FDE from a dev shop and to frame the second of his two gating questions: do you have or will you invest in a platform with shared primitives?

technologies.label: Agentic platforms
technologies.summary: Kevin Bai describes a shift in the AI era where nearly every platform has become agentic—capable of autonomous action—and customizable. This shift is central to his argument that FDE is becoming more relevant, not less: as platforms become more powerful and complex, non-technical buyers increasingly cannot understand or self-serve what the platform does, creating the exact market conditions FDE was designed for. Kevin emphasizes this is not because the industry discovered Palantir's model, but because the nature of doing business in the software industry itself changed. External sources confirm that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks are adopting FDE patterns modeled on Palantir's playbook, with the Foundry ontology pattern reportedly showing up in Claude's approach.
technologies.role: Explains why FDE matters in the AI era. Kevin uses the rise of agentic platforms to argue that FDE is not a legacy model but is becoming more relevant as AI makes platforms more complex and harder for non-technical buyers to understand.
